title: Shop database
summary: A small online shop: customers with saved addresses buy products from a tagged, nested category catalog, and each order carries its line items, a payment, and the shipments staff send out. Every one of the 14 connections is a declared foreign key; one table, audit_log, sits apart and refers to other rows only by name and id.

domains.name: Customers
domains.about: Who buys, and where they want things billed and delivered.

domains.name: Catalog
domains.about: What is for sale, how it is grouped into a category tree, and how it is tagged.

domains.name: Orders
domains.about: What each customer bought, at what price, and how they paid.

domains.name: Fulfilment
domains.about: Shipping orders out and the staff (with their reporting line) who handle it.

domains.name: Audit
domains.about: A change history that refers to rows in other tables by name, not by key.

customers.what: A person with a shop account.

columns.email: Unique across customers: a second natural key.
columns.created_at: Date the account was created (ISO text).

addresses.what: A postal address saved by a customer; one customer can save several.

columns.country: Two-letter country code, e.g. US, IN.

categories.what: A product category; categories nest inside a parent category to form a tree.

columns.parent_category_id: The enclosing category; empty for a top-level category such as Kitchen.

products.what: An item the shop sells, with its current list price.

columns.sku: Unique stock code: a second natural key.
columns.category_id: The one category the product is filed under (can be a leaf or a parent).
columns.price_cents: Current list price in cents. Order lines keep their own copy of the price paid.

tags.what: A free-form label such as gift or bestseller.

product_tags.what: A junction row saying one product carries one tag.
product_tags.grain: One row per product + tag combination.

columns.product_id: Part of the key and a foreign key to products.
columns.tag_id: Part of the key and a foreign key to tags.

orders.what: One checkout by a customer, with where to bill and where to ship.

columns.billing_address_id: Optional: empty when no separate billing address was given.

order_items.what: One line on an order: a product, how many, and the unit price charged.
order_items.grain: One row per order + line_no combination.

columns.order_id: Part of the key and a foreign key to orders.
columns.line_no: Line position within the order (1, 2, ...); only unique inside one order.
columns.unit_price_cents: Price per unit at the time of purchase, which can differ from today's products.price_cents.

payments.what: The payment taken for an order. order_id is both its primary key and its foreign key, so an order has at most one payment.

columns.order_id: Primary key and foreign key to orders at the same time.
columns.amount_cents: Amount paid in cents; in the current data it equals the order total from v_order_totals.

employees.what: A staff member; each can report to a manager who is also an employee.

columns.manager_id: The employee this person reports to; empty for the top of the hierarchy.

shipments.what: A parcel sent for an order by a carrier, optionally recorded against the employee who handled it. An order can be split over several shipments.

columns.order_id: The order this parcel belongs to; required.
columns.shipped_at: Empty until the parcel actually leaves.

audit_log.what: A record of an action (create, update, ...) performed on some row elsewhere in the database.

columns.entity: Name of the table the event is about, e.g. orders or products.
columns.entity_id: Key of that row in the table named by entity. Not a foreign key: its target changes row by row.

v_order_totals.what: Each order's value, summed from its lines (quantity times unit price). Reads orders joined to order_items.

columns.total_cents: SUM(quantity * unit_price_cents) over the order's lines.

v_customer_ltv.what: Each customer's lifetime spend: customers LEFT JOINed to v_order_totals on customer_id, so customers with no orders still appear with 0.

relationships.R1: Each address belongs to exactly one customer; a customer can have many addresses, or none.
relationships.R2: Each category sits under at most one parent category (none for a top-level category); a category can have many child categories, or none.
relationships.R3: Each employee reports to at most one manager, who is another employee (none for the top of the hierarchy); a manager can have many direct reports, or none.
relationships.R4: Each order line belongs to exactly one order; an order can have many lines, or none.
relationships.R5: Each order line is for exactly one product; a product can appear on many order lines, or none.
relationships.R6: Each order is billed to at most one address (billing is optional); an address can be the billing address of many orders, or none.
relationships.R7: Every order was placed by exactly one customer; a customer can have many orders, or none.
relationships.R8: Each order ships to exactly one address (required); an address can be the shipping address of many orders, or none.
relationships.R9: Each payment is for exactly one order; because payments.order_id is also its primary key, an order has at most one payment, or none yet.
relationships.R10: Each product-tag row names exactly one product; a product can carry many tags, or none.
relationships.R11: Each product-tag row names exactly one tag; a tag can be on many products, or none.
relationships.R12: Each product is filed under exactly one category; a category can hold many products, or none.
relationships.R13: Each shipment was handled by at most one employee (optional); an employee can handle many shipments, or none.
relationships.R14: Each shipment belongs to exactly one order; an order can have many shipments (split delivery), or none yet.

v_order_totals.answers: What was each order worth, based on its lines?

v_customer_ltv.answers: How much has each customer spent in total, including customers who never ordered?

joinPaths.question: Where was each order shipped, and who placed it?
Which products (and categories) did a customer buy?
Which tags do the products on an order carry?
Which employee handled each order's shipments? (Join employees again on manager_id to find their manager.)
Does each payment match the order's line total?

notes: orders reaches addresses two ways: billing_address_id (R6, optional) and shipping_address_id (R8, required). Always name which one you join on; joining on both at once returns only orders billed and shipped to the same address.

Nothing in the schema forces an order's billing or shipping address to belong to the same customer who placed it: R6 and R8 point at addresses, and R1 points from addresses to customers, but no constraint ties the two routes together.
Two tables point at themselves to form a hierarchy: categories (R2) and employees (R3). Walking a full tree needs a recursive query (WITH RECURSIVE), not a single join.
products and tags are many-to-many through product_tags, whose composite key (product_id, tag_id) stops the same tag being attached twice.
SQLite enforces these foreign keys only when PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON is set per connection; it was off when this file was read. PRAGMA foreign_key_check currently reports no broken links.
audit_log.entity_id is polymorphic: to join it, filter on entity first (e.g. WHERE entity = 'orders' then join orders ON order_id = entity_id). Observed entity values: orders, products.
v_customer_ltv is built on v_order_totals, so it depends on orders, order_items and customers. It counts every order regardless of status or payment.
